title: Amelia Earhart — the last radio calls, and 89 years of searching
sources: Wikipedia: Amelia Earhart — the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic (1932); in 1937 she tried to become the first woman to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan in a Lockheed Electra 10E; at Lae, New Guinea, about 22,000 miles were done and 7,000 remained, over the Pacific; on 2 July 1937 they took off for Howland Island, a strip of land 6,500 ft (2 km) long; the Coast Guard cutter Itasca waited to guide them by radio; Itasca received her voice clearly but she could not hear the ship; a radio log at 7:30–7:40 a.m. reported only half an hour of fuel left and that they could not find the ship; the US Navy searched until 19 July at a cost of $4 million; theories include a crash at sea (the government's conclusion), a castaway landing on Nikumaroro (Gardner Island) and capture by the Japanese; she was declared dead in 1939; in October 2026 an expedition by the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University examined the underwater 'Taraia Object' at Nikumaroro, which turned out to be a clump of trees.

The photo said in a 2017 TV documentary to show Earhart and Noonan in the Marshall Islands appeared in the Japanese book 'Umi no seimeisen' (1935), two years before the disappearance (both images on Wikimedia Commons).
Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / NASA / US Coast Guard): Amelia Earhart; Earhart in Darwin, 28 June 1937; Earhart with the Electra (1936); USCGC Itasca; Nikumaroro
Archive film (public domain): 'Amelia Earhart Disappears' (Pathé, 1937), 'Amelia Earhart's Flight Venture' (British Movietone, 1937), 'Amelia Earhart, Heroine of the Skies' (Pathé, 1932)
Music: Grieg, Åse's Death, public domain

post.facebook:
In 1937, the most famous pilot in the world vanished over the Pacific. 89 years later, we are still looking for her.

Amelia Earhart — the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic — set out to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan. With 22,000 miles done and 7,000 to go, on 2 July 1937 they took off from New Guinea for Howland Island, a strip of land two kilometres long in the middle of the Pacific. The Coast Guard cutter Itasca could hear her loud and clear — but she could not hear the ship. Her last calls said they were low on fuel and could not find the island. Then, silence.

The Navy searched for over two weeks and spent $4 million. Nothing. Crash at sea, castaways on a remote island, or captured by the Japanese? In 2017 a photo seemed to show them alive in Japanese hands — until it turned up in a book from 1935. And this October, an expedition to Nikumaroro checked an underwater shape that might have been her plane. It was a clump of trees.

So where is Amelia Earhart? 👇

youtube.description:
In 1937, the most famous pilot in the world vanished over the Pacific. 89 years later, we are still looking for her.

On 2 July 1937, Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan took off from Lae, New Guinea, for tiny Howland Island in their Lockheed Electra. The Coast Guard cutter Itasca heard her last radio calls — low on fuel, unable to find the island — but she could not hear the ship. A $4 million Navy search found nothing. Theories: a crash at sea, a castaway landing on Nikumaroro (Gardner Island), or capture by the Japanese. The 2017 'Jaluit photo' turned out to be from a 1935 book, and in October 2026 the underwater 'Taraia Object' at Nikumaroro turned out to be a clump of trees.
